nameStory: The 'mantled' baskettail gets its name from the dark shoulder patches on its thorax that resemble a cloak or mantle draped over its body. Like all baskettails, females have a distinctive egg-laying behavior where they dip their abdomens into the water in a basket-weaving motion, creating ripples that spread outward like a woven pattern.
description: The Mantled Baskettail is a medium-sized dragonfly with a robust, dark body and clear wings that shimmer in sunlight. Adults typically measure about 2.5 inches long with a wingspan around 3.5 inches. Their most striking feature is the dark 'mantle' or shoulder patches on their thorax, which contrasts with their metallic green-bronze body. Like other emerald dragonflies, they have large compound eyes that meet at the top of their head and powerful flight muscles that make them excellent aerial hunters.

idTips.label: Dark shoulder patches
idTips.description: Look for distinctive dark brown or black patches on the upper sides of the thorax that look like shoulder pads or a draped cloak - these feel smooth to the touch if you can observe a specimen closely

idTips.label: Metallic body coloration
idTips.description: The thorax and abdomen have a bronze-green metallic sheen that shifts color as the dragonfly moves in different light, similar to the iridescent surface of a soap bubble

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are completely transparent with dark brown wing veins and no colored patches, making a soft rustling sound when the dragonfly hovers

idTips.label: Robust body build
idTips.description: Has a thick, sturdy abdomen and thorax that feels substantial compared to more delicate damselflies - the body appears almost chunky in profile

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies in rapid, darting patterns with sudden stops and hovers, often patrolling the same stretch of water repeatedly with audible wing beats

habitat: Mantled Baskettails prefer clean, slow-moving waters like woodland ponds, beaver ponds, and quiet backwaters of streams throughout New England's forested areas. They're often found in partially shaded waters surrounded by deciduous or mixed forests, particularly where there's emergent vegetation like cattails or sedges. Adults patrol these waters for insects while nymphs develop in the muddy or silty bottom sediments.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, with fresh individuals appearing through early June. This is the best time to spot them as they're most active during their peak emergence period.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season runs from mid-June through July when adults are actively mating, egg-laying, and hunting. Look for them patrolling their territory during warm, sunny afternoons.
seasonality.fall: Activity declines significantly by August, with only occasional stragglers spotted into early September. Nymphs are developing underwater and won't emerge until the following year.
seasonality.winter: Adults are completely absent, but nymphs are actively growing in pond and stream bottoms beneath the ice, feeding on small aquatic invertebrates.

funFact: Mantled Baskettail nymphs are underwater ninjas - they can shoot out their extendable lower jaw (called a labium) at lightning speed to snatch prey, extending it up to one-third of their body length in just 25 milliseconds, faster than you can blink!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other baskettails, especially the Common Baskettail, but the Mantled Baskettail's distinctive dark shoulder patches are the giveaway - think 'mantled' equals 'shoulder pads' and you'll remember to look for those dark patches that other baskettails lack.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'emerald dragonflies,' baskettails are more bronze-green than true emerald green, and the family name can be misleading since many species appear quite dark or metallic rather than the bright green you might expect.
compareHints: Among New England baskettails, the Mantled Baskettail is the only one with prominent dark shoulder patches, making it relatively easy to distinguish. The Common Baskettail lacks these dark patches and appears more uniformly metallic, while the Prince Baskettail is larger with different thoracic markings, and the Beaverpond Baskettail has a more northern range and different habitat preferences.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the baskettails, the Beaverpond Baskettail is most closely tied to beaver-modified habitats, while the Common Baskettail prefers larger lakes and rivers, and the Prince Baskettail favors flowing streams.
Prince Baskettail is the largest of New England's baskettails and the only one with such prominent yellow markings on a brown body.
Among New England baskettails, the Common Baskettail is distinguished by its smaller size compared to Prince Baskettails and clearer wing markings than Beaverpond Baskettails.
